facts.fact_text: On 19 July 1989, the applicant joined an anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia.
According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the Nicosia District Court on 4 August 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.
While the applicant was in the Ayios Georgios chapel, she saw Turkish policemen entering the church, indiscriminately grasping women, beating them and pulling them out.
A Turkish policeman seized the applicant by one hand and twisted the other hand backwards.
A Turkish policeman pushed the applicant out of the Ayios Georgios church.
A Turkish policeman hit the applicant fiercely with a baton and with his knee in the lower part of her head and on the back of her neck as well as on other parts of her body.
The applicant was arrested and taken by bus to the so-called 'Pavlides Garage'.
On the morning of 20 July 1989 the applicant was taken to court where she was remanded in custody for forty-eight hours.
At around midnight on 22 July 1989, the court sentenced the applicant to three days' imprisonment and to a fine of CYP 50 (approximately EUR 85).

Section 70 of the Cypriot Criminal Code defines an unlawful assembly as occurring where five or more persons assemble with intent to commit an offence, or, being assembled with intent to carry out some common purpose, conduct themselves in such a manner as to cause persons in the neighbourhood to fear that the persons so assembled will commit a breach of the peace, or will by such assembly needlessly and without any reasonable occasion provoke other persons to commit a breach of the peace.
According to section 71 of the Cypriot Criminal Code, any person who takes part in an unlawful assembly is guilty of a misdemeanour and liable to imprisonment for one year.

Section 9 of Law No. 5/72 states that any person who enters a prohibited military area without authorisation, or by stealth, or fraudulently, shall be tried by a military court in accordance with the Military Offences Act, and those found guilty shall be punished.
Subsection 12(1) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that no person shall enter or leave the Colony except through an approved port.

Subsection 12(5) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that any person who contravenes or fails to observe any of the provisions of subsections (1), (2), (3) or (4) of section 12 shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months or to a fine not exceeding one hundred pounds or to both such imprisonment and fine.
The Government alleged that the applicant had participated in a violent demonstration with the aim of enflaming anti-Turkish sentiment.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators, supported by the Greek-Cypriot administration, were demanding that the 'Green Line' in Nicosia should be dismantled.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators were warned in Greek and English that unless they dispersed they would be arrested in accordance with the laws of the 'TRNC'.
According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the Nicosia District Court on 4 August 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.
While the applicant was in the Ayios Georgios chapel, she saw Turkish policemen entering the church, indiscriminately grasping women, beating them and pulling them out.
A Turkish policeman hit the applicant fiercely with a baton and with his knee in the lower part of her head and on the back of her neck as well as on other parts of her body.
During the journey to the 'Pavlides Garage', the applicant was subjected to assaults, beatings and gestures of a sexual nature by the officers who had detained her.
At the prison outside Nicosia, there were not enough mattresses and the applicant and the other detainees in her cell took turns to lie down.
The toilets and showers at the prison outside Nicosia were filthy and had no doors so the guards could see the detainees bathing.
At the court hearing around midnight on 21 July 1989, the applicant had no legal representation.
At the court hearing around midnight on 21 July 1989, prosecution witnesses lied about the basic facts surrounding the demonstration and the circumstances of the arrest.

According to the medical report of Dr. Charalambos Michael dated 28 July 1989, Mrs Despo Andreou Papi alleged that on 19 July 1989 she was hit (kicks, fists and use of police baton) on various parts of her body by Turkish pseudo-policemen in the area of Ayios Kassianos in Nicosia.

According to the medical report of Dr. Charalambos Michael dated 28 July 1989, the examination found multiple and extensive bruises on various parts of the applicant's body, particularly obvious and serious in the areas of the right buttock and the posterior surface of the left hip.

In his report of 7 December 1989 on the UN operations in Cyprus, the UN Secretary General stated that in the evening of 19 July 1989, some 1,000 Greek Cypriot demonstrators, mostly women, forced their way into the UN buffer zone in the Ayios Kassianos area of Nicosia.
According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, the demonstrators broke through a wire barrier maintained by UNFICYP and destroyed an UNFICYP observation post.
The applicant produced 21 photographs taken at different times during the demonstration on 19 July 1989.
Photographs 1 to 7 produced by the applicant were intended to show that, notwithstanding the deployment of the Turkish-Cypriot police, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.
